prompt: Two pages differ only by a timestamp in the footer and a different ad block. SHA-256 dedup treats them as distinct. Which technique detects them as near-duplicates at web scale, and how?

options.text: SimHash: a 64-bit fingerprint where similar feature sets give fingerprints with small Hamming distance, looked up via block-permuted tables to find matches within about 3 bits
options.explanation: SimHash is a candidate signal for similarity of weighted feature vectors. A small textual change does not deterministically flip only a few bits; validate thresholds and compare candidates according to the product’s false-match tolerance.
Wrong. Near-duplicate *content* often lives at completely different URLs (mirrors, printer-friendly versions). Hashing URLs can't see content similarity.

options.text: A Bloom filter of page bodies
options.explanation: Wrong. A Bloom filter tests *exact* membership. Changing one byte changes every hash, so near duplicates look completely new.

options.text: Compare every new page byte by byte against all stored pages
options.explanation: Wrong. With billions of pages, pairwise comparison is impossibly expensive. With N stored pages, each new page needs N comparisons, and the whole crawl requires a quadratic total number of comparisons: in Big O terms, O(N) per page and O(N^2) overall.

workedExample: Construct a 64-bit weighted SimHash by summing signed feature weights per bit and taking each sum’s sign. Split into four 16-bit blocks: at most three differing bits imply at least one exactly matching block by the pigeonhole principle. Use those block matches to retrieve candidates, then check full Hamming distance. Similar-content behavior is probabilistic and feature-dependent; four simple tables may produce too many candidates at billions of pages, so the paper uses more refined indexing.

link.title: Detecting near-duplicates for web crawling (Google Research)

prompt: Your URL normaliser runs before the seen-URL check. Which of these pairs should it normally map to the **same** URL? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Do not merge these blindly. UTM parameters conventionally carry analytics, but servers can use any query parameter to change the response. Strip them only after establishing site-specific equivalence.
Wrong. Paths are case-sensitive in general. Many servers return different pages (or a 404) for the two.
Correct. Scheme and host are case-insensitive, port 80 is the default for http, and fragments are never sent to the server.
Wrong as a blind rule. They often serve the same content, but not always. Rely on redirects or `rel=canonical` to merge them rather than assuming it.
Correct. Dot segments are resolved before the request is made, so both fetch `/b`.

workedExample: Normalize scheme/host case, the scheme’s default port and dot segments; omit fragments for ordinary server-side HTTP fetch identity. Do not universally lowercase paths, strip tracking-looking query parameters or merge HTTP with HTTPS. Redirects and canonical tags provide evidence/hints, not proof that all future content is identical. JavaScript fragment-routed applications may need a separate rendering identity policy.
